questions.explain: The T-SQL profiling snapshot captures null rate, distinct count, min/max, and avg length per column each night; the history of these fingerprints is what drift detection consumes.
options: A per-column statistical fingerprint — row count, null count and null_pct, distinct count, min/max values, average length — so the time series of profiles becomes a quality signal
A full copy of every table for backup purposes
Only the primary key definitions
Query execution plans for profiling queries

questions.explain: A z-score against a rolling baseline flags NULL spikes, new codes, and distribution shifts statistically — starting conservative at 4.0 and tuning down as trust builds.
options: By comparing each profile metric's latest value against a rolling baseline with a z-score, flagging deviations at z >= 4.0
By running DBCC CHECKDB daily
By alerting whenever any NULL appears in any column
By comparing table sizes to last year's backup
questions.q: How does the chapter detect data drift without hand-written rules?

questions.explain: Blocking avoids O(n^2) comparisons; the classifier trained on steward-labeled pairs scores candidates, auto-flagging >= 0.7 and routing 0.4-0.7 to humans whose decisions become retraining data.
options: DELETE all duplicates, then rebuild indexes
Exact matching on primary keys only
Full outer join of every row to every other row
Cheap T-SQL blocking (zip prefix, SOUNDEX) to narrow candidate pairs, then a RandomForest classifier scoring similarity features, with a 0.4-0.7 review band for stewards

options: They should bypass MDS to save time
They should be deleted after 7 days
They should feed MDS as intake — staged as candidates for steward approval into the golden record, keeping one write path and one approval path
MDS is only for product codes, never customers

questions.explain: The composite score blends completeness (1 - null rate), validity, uniqueness (1 - duplicate rate), and stability (1 - drift alerts); a 10-point weekly drop pages the data owner.
options: Completeness, validity, uniqueness, stability — alert when any table drops more than 10 points week over week
CPU, memory, disk, network — alert at 90% utilization
Rows, columns, indexes, partitions — alert on growth
Backups, restores, jobs, alerts — alert on failure
